title: Dan Ives Says NVDA's Recent Underperformance Is A Bump Than Anything Else — 'There's One Chip In The World Fueling The AI Revolution' - Stocktwits
content: Tech strategist Dan Ives on Monday downplayed concerns around Nvidia Corp.’s (NVDA) recent underperformance, calling it just a speed bump rather than anything else. During an interview with CNBC, Ives added that the underperformance of Nvidia and other hyperscalers is due more to the market flocking to memory stocks, calling it the “shiny new toy” effect. “You’ve seen so many of these names, when the ones that are actually at the center, whether it’s the hyperscalers or Nvidia… those are actually the ones, to some extent, almost in the penalty box,” he said. Nvidia shares were down more than 1% in Monday’s pre-market trade. Ives highlighted a disconnect between the AI trade and the companies fueling the AI revolution. “The reality is, there’s one chip in the world fueling the AI revolution, that’s by the godfather of AI the revolution, Jensen of Nvidia,” he said. Nvidia’s forward price-to-earnings ratio is currently hovering around 21.2, according to data from Koyfin, recovering slightly after falling to 19.6 last week, levels that were seen in January 2019. “When you look at memory, where is memory with Nvidia? Where's memory without hyperscalers? This all plays into what's going to be a crucial earnings season in Q2 for monetization,” he said. Ives added that he continues to see chip demand far outstripping supply, estimating the demand-to-supply ratio at 15-to-1. Ives said that the U.S. listing of SK Hynix Inc. (SKHY) is just the start, after the South Korean DRAM manufacturer raised $26.5 billion last week and debuted on Nasdaq at $170 per American Depositary Receipt (ADR), compared with an issue price of $149. “The reality is, for the first time in 30 years, the U.S. is ahead of China when it comes to tech. I think what you saw with SK, you’re going to see more and more companies tap the U.S. market,” he added. Ives also noted that the U.S. offers these companies not just liquidity but is also at the center of the AI trade. The tech strategist described Apple Inc.’s (AAPL) lawsuit against OpenAI as the iPhone maker defending its turf, adding that others in Silicon Valley will be watching what Apple does with OpenAI. “For Apple, it’s a shot across the bow. They’re basically saying, no más. This needs to stop. I think it’s important to what they’re doing, because they’re defending their turf, as well as with Google and Gemini, they finally have an AI strategy,” he said. Apple sued OpenAI in federal court in California last Friday, alleging a widespread effort to steal its trade secrets. The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI directed current and former Apple employees to provide confidential documents, product blueprints, and physical components. Apple claims the effort was orchestrated by OpenAI's leadership to accelerate the development of its own competing AI devices. NVDA stock is up 13% year-to-date and 29% over the past 12 months. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 21% over the past 12 months, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 31%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is up 136% during this period, while the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) is up 45%. Apparel companies that once represented dependable growth stories have endured a difficult five-year stretch, with major brands including Nike Inc. (NKE), Lululemon Athletica Inc. (LULU), Under Armour (UAA) and V.F. Corp. (VFC) seeing steep declines in shareholder value. After the pandemic, excess inventory, changing customer tastes, higher tariffs and lower profits turned the apparel industry from a popular investment area into a difficult market for investors. According to data from Koyfin, all the major apparel brands have recorded declines ranging from roughly 68% to more than 72% in the past five years, with the parent company of Vans and The North Face, V.F. Corp., experiencing the largest setback, losing 76.3% of its market value. The broad decline highlights how companies that once benefited from premium branding and direct consumer relationships have struggled to maintain growth as demand patterns changed. Nike entered fiscal 2026 focused on rebuilding its business after weakness in direct-to-consumer channels and declining sales in Greater China. The company recorded fiscal 2026 revenue of $46.4 billion, while fourth-quarter gross margin improved to 49.2%, partly helped by a one-time $986 million tariff recovery benefit. The company continues to focus on product improvements, inventory control and a broader restructuring effort as it prepares for a difficult fiscal 2027. During the Q2 earnings call, CEO Elliott Hill said Nike is facing slower sales in areas such as Nike Sportswear and Jordan products. Lower consumer spending, fewer store visits and increased discounting have also hurt the company and reduced future orders from retailers. China remains one of Nike’s biggest challenges. Revenue in Greater China dropped 12% to $1.3 billion in Q1, with declines across footwear, apparel and equipment sales. Nike stock edged 0.5% lower in Monday’s premarket. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bearish’ territory. Lululemon Athletica has seen its momentum slow in North America after years of rapid expansion. The company slashed its fiscal 2026 sales outlook to between $11 billion and $11.15 billion after weaker product reception and increased promotional activity pressured margins. Heidi O’Neill, a former Nike executive, is set to become the company’s permanent CEO in September as Lululemon attempts to restore growth. Lululemon Athletica stock inched 0.2% higher in Monday’s premarket. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bullish’ territory. Under Armour is working through a major restructuring led by founder and CEO Kevin Plank, with a focus on reducing discount-heavy sales and rebuilding its premium athletic image. Meanwhile, V.F. Corporation, the owner of brands such as Vans, The North Face and Timberland, has attempted to stabilize its finances through its “Reinvent” program and strategic asset sales. The companies now face the challenge of rebuilding consumer demand, improving operations and proving that their businesses can adapt to a tougher retail environment. So far this year, while UAA stock has gained 36%, VFC,  NKE and LULU stocks have declined between 7% and 42%. Ondas Holdings (ONDS) stock dropped overnight, enduring a sharp pullback that pushed the autonomous systems maker to levels not seen since late 2025, even as investors looked beyond the decline toward the company’s expanding defense operations and its push to establish a stronger position in the rapidly growing counter-drone market. Ondas stock suffered six straight weeks of decline, pushing it to a seven-month low of $7.26 on Friday, driven largely by market pressures rather than weakness in its business. The decline began after Ondas carried out several major acquisitions. To finance its rapid expansion, the company increased the number of shares it could issue, raising investor concerns about potential dilution. Short sellers increased their bets against the stock, adding further strain. According to Koyfin data, short interest in the stock was high at 33%. A share resale filing related to the Omnisys acquisition also added pressure, as it allowed some investors to sell their shares, increasing the number of shares available in the market and weighing on the stock price. Ondas stock traded more than 1% lower overnight heading into Monday. Ondas completed its $875.8 million purchase of DZYNE Technologies last week, adding a defense-focused aerospace business specializing in long-endurance autonomous aircraft and counter-unmanned systems. The deal increased Ondas’ scale and reshaped expectations around future revenue growth. The acquisition brought Ondas a business with existing operations and positive EBITDA, unlike many early-stage drone companies still working toward commercial scale. The deal included $200 million in cash and $675 million in equity. Following the DZYNE transaction, Ondas raised its 2026 revenue expectations to at least $525 million, a 34% increase from its previous guidance. Ondas’ Sentrycs unit won contracts to help protect airspace during the 2026 World Cup using its counter-drone technology. The company is also working with Lockheed Martin (LMT) to add Sentrycs technology to a defense platform that detects and counters unmanned aircraft. (HIMS) are turning investor attention toward peptides after its roughest week in two months, as it launches a new consumer campaign just days before a closely watched FDA advisory meeting. HIMS stock declined 7% last week, with shares also down over 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Late Sunday, HIMS published an Instagram carousel explaining what peptides are, why they have attracted biohackers and how they could become part of mainstream healthcare. The campaign comes as investors search for Hims’ next major growth engine beyond compounded GLP-1 drugs, and as regulators prepare to decide whether seven popular peptides should receive a clearer pathway into the U.S. compounding market. Hims said more than 170 peptides are in active clinical development, presenting the category as established science rather than a passing wellness trend. “Peptides aren’t new—they’ve been researched for decades,” the post said. “What’s changed? Research is growing, and peptides are becoming part of mainstream health conversations.” The final slide also acknowledged one of the market’s biggest challenges: inconsistent sourcing and formulation. “Not all peptides are created equal,” Hims said. “The science is real. Quality is what makes the difference.” The campaign comes ahead of the FDA’s July 23-24 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting, where members will consider adding BPC-157, Emideltide, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and TB-500 to the Section 503A Bulks List. FDA staff have recommended against all seven, citing limited human evidence, unclear formulations and unresolved risks including immune reactions and contamination. Former committee member Dr. Anita Gupta said earlier reviews raised “some red flags” over immunogenicity and pointed to reports of “heavy metals,” “microbial contamination” and mislabeling. The Partnership for Safe Medicines also urged rejection, saying the evidence is dominated by animal studies, laboratory research and weak overseas trials. It noted that BPC-157 has fewer than 36 human participants across three studies, KPV has no live-human trials and TB-500 has only one human tolerance study. The group also warned that compounding could falsely signal FDA approval and cited 127 peptide shipments entering U.S. ports in the first quarter, with about 39% coming from manufacturers outside FDA oversight. That stance contrasts with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s push for a looser approach. Kennedy has said peptides worked on his injuries with “really good effect,” while 12 peptides were moved into Category 1 in April, an early step toward possible pharmacy compounding. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) fell 3% overnight heading into Monday despite a fresh New Zealand license authorizing a gateway link for AST SpaceMobile’s expanding satellite network. ASTS stock declined 14% last week, logging its worst weekly run in over a month. The license, issued through New Zealand’s Register of Radio Frequencies, allows Two Degrees Networks to operate a space-to-Earth gateway station connected to AST SpaceMobile’s non-geostationary satellite system. The license takes effect on Monday and adds another piece of ground infrastructure to AST SpaceMobile’s direct-to-smartphone broadband network. The authorization permits a gateway, or feeder-link, earth station at a specified New Zealand site to receive signals from AST SpaceMobile satellites. It covers frequencies between 37.5 GHz and 39 GHz and limits communication to certain satellites. The conditions also require a minimum satellite elevation angle of 15 degrees and restrict operations to the approved gateway site and antenna array. AST SpaceMobile is building a low-Earth-orbit (LEO) network that can deliver voice, data and video directly to standard, unmodified smartphones. Gateway stations are a key part of the plan, as they connect satellites to terrestrial telecom networks, enabling traffic to flow between space and local mobile infrastructure. The licence comes as AST SpaceMobile prepares its next satellite deployment. The company said on Friday that BlueBird 11 had arrived at Cape Canaveral, with BlueBirds 12 and 13 expected to follow shortly ahead of a launch targeted for the first half of August. The satellites were built in Texas as AST SpaceMobile works to scale production and maintain a faster launch cadence. BlueBirds 11, 12 and 13 are expected to feature communications arrays measuring about 2,400 square feet. AST SpaceMobile said that the next-gen satellites should deliver nearly twice the peak data speeds of its first-gen Block 1 BlueBirds, which recently achieved download speeds of 98.9 Mbps directly to standard smartphones. The company is relying on stackable satellite designs and advanced composite structures to support multi-satellite launches and accelerate constellation deployment. BlueBirds 8, 9 and 10 launched from Cape Canaveral on June 17 and are now operating in orbit, placing the next three satellites in line for deployment. ASTS is targeting 45 satellites by year-end and has agreements with nearly 60 mobile-network operators representing more than 3 billion subscribers. title: S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Dip As Weaker-Than-Expected Alphabet Earnings Reignite AI Spending Worries — GOOGL, MSFT, ORCL, NVDA, MRVL In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock indices ended higher on Wednesday as the Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged helped cool some inflation worries, while weak earnings from Alphabet led the Nasdaq 100 to drop after-hours. The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.3% higher, the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.5%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, added 0.4%. Meanwhile, Nasdaq-100 futures lost 1.2%. S&P 500 futures declined 0.5%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 17 points, or 0.03% at the time of writing. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) gained 0.6%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) rose 0.2%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 0.5% higher on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF jumped about 2% each on Wednesday as gains in AMD, Micron Tech (MU) and Broadcom (AVGO). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) rose 0.6%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’, while it remained in ‘bearish’ territory for DIA and QQQ. The Federal Reserve opted to keep its target interest rate steady on Wednesday, but financial markets focused on Chair Kevin Warsh's announcement of a structural shift in the frequency of future interest rate decisions. The central bank held interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4% amid elevated inflation and a strong job market. The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10–2 vote. Under Warsh’s revamped framework, the FOMC will issue rate decisions at seven of its eight scheduled sessions in 2027, reserving one meeting exclusively for broad monetary policy strategy without issuing a formal rate statement. By 2028, the central bank plans to reduce its rate-setting votes to six per year, leaving two gatherings devoted entirely to strategic evaluations. “The Fed appears comfortable being patient for now as financial conditions have evolved broadly in line with expectations,” Luis Alvarado at Wells Fargo Investment Institute told Bloomberg. “But patience should not be confused with complacency.” Meanwhile, Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) shares slid about 11% after-hours after it reported third-quarter financial results that highlighted strong top-line revenue growth across its core digital ad and cloud operations, though massive investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and investment losses squeezed profitability. These corporate reports arrive as Wall Street sharpens its focus on the artificial intelligence ecosystem. Following a prolonged pullback throughout much of October, AI-linked funds like the iShares Semiconductor ETF and the Roundhill Memory ETF have mounted a fresh rebound in recent trading sessions. Oracle Corp. (ORCL) share price rallied about 11% on Wednesday, closing its best day since May this year, after executives unveiled a net cash-flow-positive outlook, helping alleviate capex concerns. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) share price inched 3% higher after-hours on Wednesday after the software maker’s first-quarter results surpassed Wall Street expectations, propelled by surging demand for its artificial intelligence tools and cloud computing platform. Shares of Nvidia Corp (NVDA) slipped 1% on Wednesday  following reports that the U.S. Department of Justice has inquired about how its planned acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in artificial intelligence. Shares of Lumentum Holdings Inc (LITE) soared 10% after hours on Wednesday following a report that Marvell Technology is in talks to buy it in a potential megadeal. Shares of Lumentum Holdings Inc (LITE) soared 10% after hours on Wednesday following a report that Marvell Technology is in talks to buy it in a potential megadeal. A deal between Marvell and the data center optics maker could be announced as soon as next week, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed people familiar with the matter. A final deal hasn’t been reached, and details could change, the report said. After Wednesday’s market close, Lumentum has a market value of about $83 billion, while Marvell is valued near $221 billion. Shares of MRVL tumbled 8% following the report. Marvell is a fabless semiconductor designer focused on data-infrastructure solutions, while Lumentum makes optical and photonic products such as lasers, optical components, and networking systems used in cloud and AI data centers. Lumentum’s indium-phosphide technology is particularly in high demand; CEO Michael Hurlston has previously said that the company is essentially sold out of certain products into 2029 and is under-shipping demand by substantial margins due to the fast-paced nature of AI data center buildouts. Marvell, too, is strengthening its position in  the AI space, recently inking a partnership with Google on custom chips. Shares of Nvidia Corp (NVDA) slipped 1% on Wednesday  following reports that the U.S. Department of Justice has inquired about how its planned acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in artificial intelligence. According to a report from Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, department officials have asked whether the Hugging Face deal would allow Nvidia to control a key distribution point for AI models and tools. The questioning adds to the years-long probe by antitrust regulators on Nvidia’s conduct, which kicked off under former President Joe Biden, the report said. The probe is reportedly continuing with no indication that current President Donald Trump has any involvement. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a relationship with Trump and recently joined the President on his diplomatic trip to China. The DOJ’s recent line of questioning covers the company’s acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether it has pressured customers, sources told Reuters. As part of the probe, the DOJ has reportedly examined Nvidia’s other acquisition deals, including the December 2025 deal to buy SchedMD, sources told Reuters. The department has also scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its licensing deal with chip startup Groq and its acquisition of Run.ai, the report added. Nvidia announced in early September that it had agreed to buy Hugging Face for approximately $12.93 billion. The transaction includes roughly $11.9 billion payable to Hugging Face’s investors and an equity-based retention program of up to about $1 billion for employees who join Nvidia. Hugging Face operates a widely used platform that hosts millions of open-source AI models, datasets, and applications, serving millions of developers and hundreds of thousands of companies. It is often described as a central hub for open AI development. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pledged that the platform will remain open to models, frameworks, clouds, and computing platforms from across the industry, and that Nvidia’s own chips will not be required to use it. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Shares of Hims & Hers (HIMS) jumped 5% on Wednesday after the Department of Health and Human Services said it would temporarily allow compounding pharmacies to produce six popular peptides. HHS said it will not go after state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities, or licensed doctors for compounding six peptides—BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500—as long as they follow basic rules on ingredient quality, manufacturing, safety reporting, labeling, and prescriptions written for individual patients. “...based on the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting and data regarding utilization of peptides, HHS believes that there is significant interest in the use of these peptides in compounding,” HHS said, referring to the advisory committee recommendation in July that some peptides be considered for compounding. The new policy is temporary while the FDA completes formal rulemaking on the official list of bulk substances that can be used in compounding. Compounders must report serious adverse events with the use of the drugs or any product quality issues such as contamination to the FDA, HHS added.  Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Hims has already prepared for a potential approval of peptide compounding by securing a California peptide facility and testing ingredients, while signaling interest in offering items such as sermorelin, glutathione, and NAD+ depending on final regulatory outcomes. Peptides used for recovery, inflammation, sleep, and related wellness goals have drawn strong consumer interest online, even without formal FDA approval. “We have spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own US-based peptide manufacturing facility, developing dosing protocols with clinical experts, and setting up frameworks to better understand these emerging treatments,” the company’s Chief Medical Officer Anant Vinjamoori said after the HHS directive in a post on X. HIMS CEO Andrew Dudum also termed it “encouraging progress.” HIMS, however, has also faced setbacks this year, including an FTC lawsuit filed in late July alleging deceptive privacy practices involving data sharing with advertising platforms and misleading billing or cancellation practices. The company transitioned from offering compounded GLP-1s to branded versions earlier this year, pressuring margins despite subscriber growth. One of the liveliest ongoing debates on Wall Street is whether artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending will continue to grow at a good clip over the medium term. If it doesn't, some industry leaders will see revenue and earnings growth slow, and their share prices could sink. But if it does, some AI-focused companies still have plenty of room to run. Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), recently made comments that support the bullish outlook. Of course, Huang is hardly an unbiased observer. Still, it's worth paying attention to what he said and the potential implications for Nvidia and other AI leaders. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » First, a little bit of background on neocloud companies. Unlike traditional cloud computing providers like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) that offer a broad range of services, neoclouds specialize in renting out the compute power needed to develop and run AI models. Neoclouds became more prominent as the AI revolution took off, but there is more room for them to grow, at least if we believe the words of Jensen Huang. In a recent interview, the CEO of Nvidia said: If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary, and so what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth, to fund that growth. There is a lot to unpack here. First, the great news. Demand for neocloud services being off the charts is a bullish sign for Nvidia. These neoclouds purchase GPUs (graphics processing units) from the company and rent out GPU compute to other corporations. Growing demand could force these companies to expand their capacity. That means they may keep buying Nvidia's GPUs. But can they afford this massive AI build-out? That's the not-so-great news. As Huang pointed out, these companies may lack the capital necessary to purchase the infrastructure -- including GPUs -- to meet demand for their services. Recent developments support Huang's view. Companies like CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) and even Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) have said that there is more demand for their services than they can (or are willing to) provide, at least in the short term. Meanwhile, CoreWeave has raised more than $30 billion in debt and equity capital this year. Note that the company is worth about $33 billion as of writing, so it has raised capital equivalent to almost 91% of its market cap in a single year. That points to the financial bottleneck Huang mentioned and to how some neocloud companies are looking to solve it. But what does all this mean for Nvidia's prospects? One bullish scenario could go like this. CoreWeave and its neocloud peers will conjure up various ways to fund their massive AI build-outs. Perhaps they will borrow more, or resort to dilutive forms of financing (or both). Another possibility is that more competitors will enter the market upon seeing the massive, lucrative opportunity. The result: neocloud companies will continue to purchase the infrastructure necessary to meet demand for their services, and some of that money will flow directly into Nvidia's pockets. Of course, this also assumes that the AI boom will continue unabated at least over the next few years. If it doesn't, neoclouds could significantly reduce spending, leading to lower demand for Nvidia's products. Which scenario is more likely? Probably something closer to the first one. Soaring demand for neocloud services, the growing popularity of AI agents, and several other indicators support this. Medium-term projections for AI infrastructure spending remain high for these (and other) reasons. And Nvidia could be one of the biggest winners. So, it's not too late to invest in the stock, even after its amazing run in recent years. title: Here's What $10,000 Invested Equally in SpaceX and Nvidia Could Be Worth in 2030 - The Motley Fool
content: A $10,000 investment in SpaceX and Nvidia could rise fivefold by 2030. Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -6.37%) are two of the most exciting artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, and with SpaceX deciding to build its data centers exclusively on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, the two companies are inextricably linked. With $10,000 split between the two stocks, investors could buy 34 shares of SpaceX and 23 shares of Nvidia. With SpaceX set to ramp up its compute capacity to levels never seen before, a $10,000 investment split between the two stocks could be worth over $52,000 by the end of 2030. Here's how. SpaceX has seen some of the best returns on its AI infrastructure investments, with a payback breakeven in about a year. Meanwhile, CEO Elon Musk thinks the company can push that down to around six months. With that type of return profile, SpaceX is set to embark on one of the largest AI infrastructure investments ever seen. Musk said the company plans to end this year with up to 3 gigawatts of computing power and end 2027 with at least 13 gigawatts. Meanwhile, it has a long-shot goal of adding up to an incremental 20 gigawatts of computing capacity next year. One gigawatt of power costs approximately $50 billion to build on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, so SpaceX is looking to spend at least $500 billion in capital expenditures (capex) next year on AI infrastructure, with the potential to spend up to $1 trillion. Meanwhile, Musk has projected that this could help SpaceX end 2027 with between $500 billion and $1 trillion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Now, let's say SpaceX adds 10 gigawatts of compute capacity each of the next five years; that would give the company 53 gigawatts of computing power at the end of 2031. Assuming similar revenue per gigawatt, that would be a year-end 2031 ARR of around $2.65 trillion. Throw in SpaceX's Starlink, increased rocket launches, and AI coding growth, and it could hit $3 trillion in revenue in 2031. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Place a 5 times price-to-sales (P/S) multiple on the stock, and it would be worth $15 trillion. However, all this capex will lead to a higher share count, which we'll assume will be diluted by 10% in 2027, gradually stepping down by 1% a year. This would lead to a $750 share price, and those 34 shares would be worth $25,500 by the end of 2030. Nvidia gets roughly $40 billion per gigawatt in revenue from its Vera Rubin architecture. This comes not only from its graphics processing units (GPUs), but also from its networking components, other chips -- such as central processing units (CPUs) and inference language processing units (LPUs) -- and its expanding software layer that goes into the configuration of its Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale supercomputing platform. As such, if SpaceX adds 10 gigawatts of power a year, it would equate to around $400 billion in annual revenue just from one customer. However, Nvidia obviously has a lot of customers and has been growing rapidly. Nvidia has also been able to get more revenue per gigawatt with each new generation of its architecture, going from approximately $18 billion for Hopper to $25 billion for Grace Blackwell, and now $40 billion with Vera Rubin. There is good reason to believe this will continue. As such, I think Nvidia's current analyst estimates will likely prove too low. If Nvidia can sell more Vera Rubin systems to SpaceX without missing out on selling capacity to other customers, its fiscal 2028 revenue could be closer to $850 billion. That would take my model to the company generating adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of nearly $61 in fiscal 2032 (ending January). Place a 19 times forward P/E on that, which is a current S&P 500 market multiple, and the stock would be worth $1,160 by the end of 2030. Meanwhile, those 23 shares would be worth roughly $26,650. title: Should You Buy, Sell, or Hold Nvidia Stock in 2026? - LiteFinance
content:
Over the past five years, Nvidia shares have surged more than 1,100%, propelling the company to the top of global market capitalization by the end of 2025, surpassing Apple. However, growth slowed in 2025, with competitors such as Intel, Broadcom, and AMD delivering higher returns. This raises a key question for investors: should they continue to hold Nvidia shares, or is the stock overvalued, making it more prudent to explore undervalued opportunities? This review offers insights into whether to buy, hold, or sell Nvidia shares in 2026. Nvidia is one of the world's leading companies in the semiconductor sector. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are used in robotics, cloud computing, neural network development, machine learning, and AI, as well as in automated systems. Over the past five years, Nvidia's stock has gained 1,325%, making it the world's largest company by market capitalization by the end of 2025, overtaking Apple. In 2025, NVIDIA delivered a stock return of 53.26%, lower than those of its main competitors: AMD, Broadcom, and Intel. For the next five years, the company has forged strategic partnerships with major tech firms such as Meta and Samsung, while investing billions of dollars in OpenAI and other innovative startups. NVDA shares are expected to continue appreciating, though likely at a more moderate pace. The stock remains suitable for diversifying a long-term investment portfolio. Nvidia shares are listed on the NASDAQ stock exchange under the ticker #NVDA. On the LiteFinance trading platform, you can trade them Monday through Friday, from 15:35 to 22:00 (GMT+2). Stock exchanges are closed on weekends, but #NVDAx perpetual contracts are available for trading 24/7. In 2025, Nvidia delivered record-breaking financial results, in line with analysts' expectations. Price-to-Earnings (P/E): 36.77 – Although this figure is high, it still lags behind levels seen in previous periods. The market average ranges from 20 to 25. For fast-growing tech companies, such a P/E is acceptable, reflecting market expectations of strong future earnings growth. For Nvidia, the elevated P/E reflects expectations of growing demand for chips used in AI and data centers. Forward P/E: 16.51 – Significantly lower than the current P/E, this indicates that analysts expect a sharp increase in earnings. The market suggests the company's earnings could nearly double, indicating potential undervaluation. PEG Ratio: 0.43 – A value below 1 is generally considered a sign of undervaluation. In this case, earnings growth is more than twice the pace of stock price growth, signaling strong expected earnings momentum in the coming years. Regarding other financial metrics, the company is outperforming the industry average by a significant margin. Is NVDA a good stock to buy? The answer depends on your investment goals. title: Apple (AAPL.US) overtakes NVIDIA (NVDA.US) to regain top spot in global market capitalization, as its relatively restrained capital expenditure wins market favor. - 富途牛牛
content: From Apple to Eli Lilly and Co, what are the AI-driven hedging strategies? As concerns on Wall Street about the hefty returns on tech giants' massive investments in artificial intelligence (AI) continue to mount,$Apple (AAPL.US)$Surpass on Friday$NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$, once again becoming the world's most valuable publicly traded company. Amid widespread sell-offs in tech stocks, Apple has emerged as a more defensive choice for investors, thanks to its relatively restrained capital expenditures and robust cash flow. On Friday, Apple's stock fell 1.2%, closing with a market capitalization of about $5.03 trillion; NVIDIA's shares dropped 4.2%, bringing its market cap down to $4.93 trillion. This marks the first time Apple has reclaimed the top spot on the global market-cap leaderboard since briefly surpassing NVIDIA at the end of July this year. Behind Apple's regaining the top spot in market capitalization lies a shift in the market's attitude toward the AI investment prospects of tech giants. Recently,$Intel (INTC.US)$ 、$Amazon (AMZN.US)$、 $Alphabet-A (GOOGL.US)$and$Meta Platforms (META.US)$As major tech companies have successively released disappointing financial results or earnings guidance, investors have grown concerned about the growth prospects of the tech sector and the returns on AI investments. Notably, as major tech companies continue to pour substantial capital into building AI data centers and other computing infrastructure, the market is beginning to question whether these investments can generate sufficient revenue and profits within a reasonable timeframe. Some tech giants' capital expenditures have already exceeded their operating cash flows, resulting in negative free cash flow. Both Alphabet and Amazon are experiencing this situation and are increasingly relying on the bond market to finance their investments. Meanwhile, rising interest rates are further driving up companies' financing costs. In contrast, Apple has not made large-scale investments in AI infrastructure like other tech giants, instead maintaining a relatively restrained capital expenditure strategy. This has won it favor from investors as the market re-evaluates the risks of AI investments. Data shows that Apple's stock has risen 27% year-to-date, making it not only the best-performing stock among the U.S. "Big Seven," but also outpacing NVIDIA, which ranks second, by more than double. Meanwhile, Apple's cash flow performance has also significantly surpassed that of some of its tech peers. The market expects Apple's free cash flow to grow 38% year over year in fiscal year 2026, which ends on September 30, reaching $142 billion. Strong cash flow means that Apple can support its business growth and shareholder returns without resorting to large-scale borrowing, unlike some of its competitors. Against the backdrop of rising interest rates and increasing financing costs for tech companies, this advantage is attracting growing attention from investors. As Apple regained the top spot in global market capitalization, the U.S. tech sector is undergoing a noticeable correction. Following a sharp plunge on Friday, the stock has posted a cumulative drop of over 45% in October, marking the largest monthly decline in more than four decades of data compiled by Bloomberg. Overall, Apple has once again surpassed NVIDIA, reflecting a shift in how investors evaluate large tech companies. Previously, the market favored firms that aggressively invested in AI infrastructure and could capitalize on the AI boom; now, as capital expenditures continue to rise and financing costs increase, investors are placing greater emphasis on corporate cash flow, profitability, and financial stability. title: Why Nvidia Stock Took a Dive Today - The Motley Fool
content: The AI chipmaker sparked renewed fears of circular AI financing. Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) was part of a broad sell-off in the tech sector on Friday, with shares falling as much as 5.3%. As of 2:11 p.m. ET, the stock was still down 5.2%. While the tech downdraft was certainly a contributor, the catalyst that sent the chipmaker lower was the rising cost of artificial intelligence (AI) and the question of who will pay for it all. Reports emerged today that Nvidia may be considering another financing deal with a customer. The company is reportedly in talks to provide billions of dollars in credit guarantees for an Nscale data center that will ultimately be used by Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, which cited "a person familiar with the matter." This marks the latest in a growing string of financing and credit commitments Nvidia has made. For example, reports from earlier this week suggest the company has data center-related commitments and guarantees of $165 billion, according to a report that first appeared in The Information. That's not all. Nvidia also holds more than $63 billion in equity stakes in publicly traded companies, according to a recent regulatory filing. Many of those stakes are in the chipmaker's customers, either directly or indirectly. When you include start-ups, that figure climbs to $99 billion. This has fueled fears among some investors of the repercussions if AI adoption slows or someone builds a better mousetrap than Nvidia's industry-leading graphics processing units (GPUs). If that were to happen, it could be the catalyst that starts the dominoes falling, and the AI trade could all unravel -- or so the popular narrative goes. Yet a look at Nvidia's recent financials should help put those fears to rest. For the company's fiscal 2027 second quarter (ended July 26), the chipmaker generated revenue of $96 billion, up 106% year over year -- and expects that figure to rise to $108 billion when it reports its Q3 results in mid-November. Moreover, Nvidia carries more than $99 billion in cash and marketable securities on its balance sheet, which, in my opinion, provides sufficient liquidity to cover its various financing and credit commitments. We'll have more details when Nvidia releases its next earnings report after the market close on Nov. 17. At less than 26 times earnings, Nvidia stock hasn't been this cheap since 2019. title: The Smartest AI Stock to Buy on Anthropic's IPO Filing Isn't Anthropic - The Motley Fool
content: Anthropic is exciting, but Nvidia is a guaranteed winner. Anthropic has filed its S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which signals its intent to go public in the future. Some of the information in this document is incredible, ranging from AI risks to the sheer amount of money Anthropic plans to spend over the next few years. However, there's one overarching theme that prevails in the S-1 document that makes me want to invest in a different stock entirely: Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%). Nvidia has been the undisputed leader among AI investments since this trend started in 2023. However, it hasn't done as well recently, even though its business is booming. Seeing Anthropic's S-1 filing gave me confidence that Nvidia's still a great stock to buy, and that now could be the perfect buying opportunity. Anthropic lists several major industry partners, including Nvidia. Anthropic uses multiple chips to train and run its AI models, and can easily select the cheapest option for the given workload. Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are also used heavily in cloud computing environments, as companies that are hosting an internal AI model or creating a product that has Anthropic's Claude as its AI backbone will need to pay for their own cloud computing costs. These workloads also use Nvidia GPUs, so it's clear that Nvidia's products are being used all over the place. Anthropic also has lots of commentary about the length of time its spending will last, often citing timeframes that are five to 10 years out. That pretty clearly shows that, in Anthropic's view, the AI build-out is a long way from wrapping up. Nvidia supports that thesis, as it believes global AI data center capital expenditures will rise to $3 trillion to $4 trillion annually by 2030. Anthropic will be a major part of that figure, and all that will add up to Nvidia's business continuing to expand. However, the market doesn't believe it, even if it's looking it directly in the face. Nvidia has already given strong guidance for 70% revenue growth in 2027. The problem is, the market hasn't factored a single penny of growth into its stock price beyond 2026. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Nvidia trades for about 23 times this year's earnings estimates. If you use next year's, that figure tumbles to a dirt cheap 13.6 times earnings. This is due to the sheer volume of computing capacity that has yet to be deployed to run an AI-first society. Nvidia is by far the largest computing provider in this area. This will provide huge growth opportunities for many years, and makes it one of the best AI stocks to buy now, if not the best. It's rare to find a company expected to grow at 70% in the next fiscal year, trading at just 27 times earnings, but that's exactly the value Nvidia offers. The market doesn't want to believe that AI spending will remain strong over the next year, but that's likely what will happen unless something drastic changes in the market. I think this is a pretty safe investment with huge upside, and there are few better stocks for investors to scoop up than Nvidia right now. Anthropic is just one of Nvidia's valued clients, and its S-1 has provided more information about massive AI spending in 2027. Other companies will announce 2027 spending plans soon and should confirm the Nvidia bull case. NVIDIA announced a broad slate of AI platforms, including the OpenShell Reference Architecture, DSX POD modular AI factories and RTX Spark PCs, alongside expanded collaborations with Oracle, Meta and industrial partners to scale AI training, inference and agent workloads across cloud, data center and edge environments. The news highlights NVIDIA's push to move from selling chips to supplying full AI factory blueprints, from liquid-cooled Vera Rubin clusters down to on-device RTX Spark systems, tightening its role in how customers design, deploy and govern large scale AI infrastructure. We will look at how NVIDIA's shift toward full-stack AI factories, highlighted by DSX POD, could shape its long-term investment narrative. The biggest risk right now is not demand; it is concentration and competition. Large cloud customers are pushing in house accelerators, and regulators are scrutinizing deals like Hugging Face. The latest Oracle expansion strengthens NVIDIA's role in third party AI infrastructure and therefore supports the core thesis rather than changing it. The Oracle Cloud Infrastructure announcement is the clearest read through for NVIDIA's AI factory story. Scaling OCI superclusters with Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs, plus Spectrum X networking, ties directly into the idea that revenue per gigawatt rises as customers adopt full stack Vera Rubin platforms instead of buying stand alone GPUs. Operationally, the Oracle deal matters because it lets customers scale CPU and GPU capacity independently. This aligns well with agentic workloads that are relatively GPU light but CPU hungry between model calls. That supports the key catalyst that AI factories need both accelerators and Vera CPUs at scale, while leaving intact the risk that over time, hyperscalers could still shift part of that stack to their own silicon. The current consensus assumes NVIDIA's top line grows by 48.7% a year over the next three years, even as profit margins move from 63.7% today toward 54.3% in three years. That mix of rapid sales expansion and lower profitability per dollar of revenue sketches a future where scale matters more than peak margin, which fits the AI factory framing of Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell clusters serving enormous workloads for hyperscalers, neoclouds and industrial customers. On earnings, analysts expect net profit to move from US$192.9b today to US$540.6b by 2029. However, there are many new investment options in the AI world, including Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX). SpaceX has a major AI wing thanks to its acquisition of xAI before going public, and this division has delivered incredible growth. In fact, it has some investors wondering if it's one of the best AI investments on the market right now. But is it better than Nvidia? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Nvidia makes graphics processing units (GPUs), which are broad-purpose computing units that excel in nearly any environment. This makes them extremely flexible, and with Nvidia's GPUs being recognized as the best available, they're quite popular. In fact, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture is the best available and that SpaceX will exclusively deploy Nvidia's products for its AI endeavors. That's a pretty notable endorsement, and it solidifies the relationship between these two. SpaceX's AI product centers around its Grok large language model. This has become a popular model to use because it's connected to X, which helps it understand current events. It also offers other products like Grok Bots, which are becoming popular because they give users access to AI agents that can handle tasks on their behalf. Nvidia and SpaceX are two distinct investments, as Nvidia is on the infrastructure side, and SpaceX is on the application side. Although there's still a lot of AI computing infrastructure to build, companies are starting to move into the application phase of AI, which may favor SpaceX delivering better results. That's exactly what we're seeing now, as SpaceX just blew expectations out of the water in the third quarter. During Q3, SpaceX's Super Intelligence (SI) division (the new name of its AI division) saw revenue increase at a jaw-dropping 830% rate. While this quarter's results included an acquisition that boosted the segment's overall growth rate, it was still a monster quarter for SpaceX. SpaceX is more focused on capturing market share, so it doesn't care a lot about profitability. Still, its operating income for its AI division was $431 million on revenue of $7.56 billion, good for a 5.7% margin. On the flip side, Nvidia's operating margin for its most recent quarter was 66%. This means that Nvidia is producing huge profits while SpaceX's are comparatively minimal. That should be expected based on the phase each company is in. Still, the speed at which Nvidia is already growing, combined with incredible profitability, causes me to prefer Nvidia's financial picture. Because SpaceX is barely profitable, I think valuing it based on expected sales this year makes the most sense. Right now, SpaceX has a market cap of $2 trillion, and Wall Street expects 2026 revenue of $48.6 billion. That equates to a forward price-to-sales ratio of about 41. Nvidia is expected to generate $411.7 billion in revenue this year. With a market cap of $5.1 trillion, Nvidia's stock is priced at just 12 times sales. title: NVDA's Gross Margin Faces Pressure: Can It Offset Rising Memory Costs? - The Globe and Mail
content: NVIDIA Corporation’s NVDA gross margins could face pressure as rising memory costs and supply constraints challenge its ability to maintain strong profitability. However, the company’s pricing power, growing AI demand and shift toward advanced platforms could help offset some of these headwinds. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, NVIDIA reported a non-GAAP gross margin of 75% compared with 72.4% a year earlier and 75% in the previous quarter. Revenues jumped 106% year over year and 18% sequentially to $96.2 billion, while Data Center revenues surged 117% to $89 billion. These figures highlight the company’s strong position in the AI infrastructure market. Still, NVIDIA expects gross margin to decline sequentially to 74% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, plus or minus 50 basis points. Higher memory prices are a key concern because advanced AI systems require large amounts of high-performance memory. Tight supply could increase component costs and limit production flexibility. NVIDIA has several ways to protect profitability. Its strong relationships with major memory suppliers could help secure supplies, while its advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) and integrated computing systems give it pricing power. The company is also increasing supply and capacity commitments to support future demand. The Vera Rubin platform offers another potential boost. Its improved computing performance and efficiency could help customers justify higher spending on AI infrastructure, supporting NVIDIA’s ability to pass on some cost increases. Overall, NVIDIA’s margins may face near-term pressure, but strong demand and pricing power provide important support. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.AMD and Intel CorporationINTC are expanding their AI businesses, but rising component costs and production challenges could affect their profitability. Advanced Micro Devices reported second-quarter 2026 revenues of $11.54 billion, up 13% quarter over quarter, while its non-GAAP gross margin reached 56.2% compared with 55% in the first quarter. Its Data Center revenues climbed 16% sequentially to $6.7 billion, supported by demand for EPYC processors and Instinct GPUs. However, Advanced Micro Devices’ third-quarter guidance indicates gross margin will remain flat sequentially. For the third quarter, it anticipates non-GAAP gross margin to be 56% in the third quarter. To continue improving margins, AMD must maintain cost control as it scales AI chip production. title: NVDA Stock Retreats as Google TPUs and Nvidia Debt Risk Challenge the Growth Outlook - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia stock retreated after rebounding, with resistance at $220 as Google’s expanding TPU business, rising financing costs and data-centre power shortages raise questions about the sustainability of semiconductor demand. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares recovered towards $220 after falling to $210 last Friday, but the rebound has struggled to gain traction following an earlier retreat from record highs above $243. The stock is pulling back again despite improving sentiment across parts of the semiconductor sector, as investors reassess the costs and risks associated with expanding computing infrastructure. Expectations of persistent memory shortages and higher prices have supported chipmakers, but strong demand alone may not guarantee continued growth. Nvidia’s customers must secure sufficient financing, electricity and operational capacity to deploy increasingly expensive processors. The central concern is whether technology companies can convert substantial infrastructure commitments into profitable services before rising costs and competitive pressures undermine returns. Google’s expanding custom-chip business presents another challenge. On Tuesday, Google and Oracle announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. The agreement marks the first time Google’s TPUs will be offered through another hyperscale cloud platform. The arrangement could give Oracle customers an alternative to Nvidia-powered computing systems, particularly for workloads suited to Google’s specialised processors. Nvidia retains significant advantages through its established software ecosystem, broad customer base and high-performance GPU platform. However, Google’s move demonstrates how major technology companies are seeking greater flexibility over computing costs and hardware supply. If custom chips become increasingly competitive, Nvidia could face pressure on pricing and market share in selected applications, even if overall computing demand continues to grow. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that planned semiconductor manufacturing capacity in 2027 and 2028 might not fully meet anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Its US-listed shares reportedly fell approximately 4%, adding pressure to semiconductor stocks. Manufacturing constraints could support chip prices, but they may also delay the equipment required to expand production. For Nvidia, supply limitations can complicate customers’ deployment schedules and restrict how quickly additional computing capacity becomes operational. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently.
